blocks.es_reference: 📖 Predicación Doctrinal — Unidad 10: Predicando la Doctrina de las Últimas Cosas

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "...we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is." — 1 John 3:2 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "...seremos semejantes a Él, porque le veremos como Él es." — 1 Juan 3:2 (RVG)

blocks.en: Day 1 — Why End the Course Here
blocks.es_reference: Día 1 — Por qué terminar aquí el curso

blocks.en: Every other doctrine has prepared for this one. Revelation told us God has spoken; God, Man, Christ, the Spirit, Salvation, and the Church have unfolded His work; and now Last Things tells us where it is all going. This is the doctrine of hope, and it is the natural close of a preaching course because it is where every faithful sermon finally points: to the return of Christ and the world to come.
blocks.es_reference: Toda otra doctrina ha preparado para esta. La Revelación nos dijo que Dios ha hablado; Dios, el Hombre, Cristo, el Espíritu, la Salvación y la Iglesia han desplegado su obra; y ahora las Últimas Cosas nos dicen hacia dónde va todo. Esta es la doctrina de la esperanza, y es el cierre natural de un curso de predicación porque es a donde apunta finalmente todo sermón fiel: al regreso de Cristo y al mundo venidero.

blocks.en: But it is also the doctrine most often preached badly — turned into a chart of dates, a map of current events, a contest of theories. The pastoral aim is the opposite: to comfort the grieving, to sober the careless, and to fix the hearer’s hope on Christ Himself rather than on a timeline.
blocks.es_reference: Pero también es la doctrina que más a menudo se predica mal — convertida en un cuadro de fechas, un mapa de los sucesos actuales, un concurso de teorías. El objetivo pastoral es lo contrario: consolar al que llora, despertar al descuidado, y fijar la esperanza del oyente en Cristo mismo en lugar de en una cronología.

blocks.en: "...we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is." — 1 John 3:2 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "...seremos semejantes a Él, porque le veremos como Él es." — 1 Juan 3:2 (RVG)

blocks.en: Day 2 — The Doctrinal Backbone (lean; see Systematic Theology Unit 10)
blocks.es_reference: Día 2 — El fundamento doctrinal (breve; vea Teología Sistemática, Unidad 10)

blocks.en: Hold the doctrine; keep it compressed and point students to ST Unit 10. Death is not the end but a doorway; the believer who dies is “absent from the body and present with the Lord.” The return of Christ is personal, visible, and certain — He will come again as He went. The resurrection raises the body; our hope is not a disembodied soul but a redeemed and glorified body. The judgment is real: all will stand before God. The final state is eternal — the unbroken joy of God’s presence for those who are His, or the everlasting loss of it for those who are not. Hold these five together and you have the whole hope: the believer who dies is at once with the Lord; the Lord Himself will return in person; the body will be raised and not merely the soul preserved; every life will be weighed before God; and the end is not annihilation but eternity, on one side of that presence or the other. None of this is morbid speculation — it is the spine of Christian hope, and the reason a believer can stand at a graveside and not grieve as those who have none. The course holds these humbly and non-denominationally, distinguishing the certainties (He will return; the dead will rise; we shall be like Him) from the disputed details of timing and sequence, and it refuses to let the disputes crowd out the hope.
blocks.es_reference: Sostenga la doctrina; manténgala comprimida y remita a los alumnos a la Unidad 10 de TS. La muerte no es el fin sino una puerta; el creyente que muere está “ausente del cuerpo y presente con el Señor.” El regreso de Cristo es personal, visible y cierto — vendrá otra vez como se fue. La resurrección levanta el cuerpo; nuestra esperanza no es un alma sin cuerpo sino un cuerpo redimido y glorificado. El juicio es real: todos compareceremos ante Dios. El estado final es eterno — el gozo ininterrumpido de la presencia de Dios para los que son suyos, o la pérdida eterna de ella para los que no lo son. Sostenga estas cinco verdades juntas y tendrá toda la esperanza: el creyente que muere está al instante con el Señor; el Señor mismo volverá en persona; el cuerpo será resucitado y no solo preservada el alma; cada vida será pesada ante Dios; y el fin no es la aniquilación sino la eternidad, de un lado de esa presencia o del otro. Nada de esto es especulación morbosa — es la espina dorsal de la esperanza cristiana, y la razón por la cual un creyente puede estar junto a una tumba y no afligirse como los que no tienen esperanza. El curso sostiene esto con humildad y sin denominacionalismo, distinguiendo las certezas (Él volverá; los muertos resucitarán; seremos semejantes a Él) de los detalles disputados de tiempo y secuencia, y se niega a dejar que las disputas desplacen la esperanza.

blocks.en: Day 3 — The Homiletical Move (the worked example from Unit 2, now developed)
blocks.es_reference: Día 3 — El movimiento homilético (el ejemplo de la Unidad 2, ahora desarrollado)

blocks.en: Back in Unit 2 we sketched this outline to show how a subject becomes points. Now we develop it as a finished sermon. Subject: the return of Christ. Interrogative: the doctrine answers the questions every honest heart asks. Keyword: questions. Three points, each a question with its own text:
blocks.es_reference: Allá en la Unidad 2 esbozamos este bosquejo para mostrar cómo un tema se vuelve puntos. Ahora lo desarrollamos como sermón terminado. Tema: el regreso de Cristo. Interrogativo: la doctrina responde a las preguntas que todo corazón honesto hace. Palabra clave: preguntas. Tres puntos, cada uno una pregunta con su propio texto:

blocks.en: Point (keyword: questions)Anchor text
blocks.es_reference: Punto (palabra clave: preguntas)Texto base

blocks.en: 1. When will He come? — No one knows; be readyMatthew 24:36, 44
blocks.es_reference: 1. ¿Cuándo vendrá? — Nadie lo sabe; estad listosMateo 24:36, 44

blocks.en: 2. What will happen when He comes? — The dead rise, we are gathered1 Thessalonians 4:16–17
blocks.es_reference: 2. ¿Qué pasará cuando venga? — Los muertos resucitan, somos reunidos1 Tesalonicenses 4:16–17

blocks.en: 3. What will we become? — We shall be like Him1 John 3:2
blocks.es_reference: 3. ¿Qué llegaremos a ser? — Seremos semejantes a Él1 Juan 3:2

blocks.en: Notice the deliberate order. The first question humbles our curiosity (we are not told the date). The second steadies our grief (death does not win). The third lifts our hope to its height (we shall be like Christ) — and that is where the sermon should peak.
blocks.es_reference: Note el orden deliberado. La primera pregunta humilla nuestra curiosidad (NO se nos dice la fecha). La segunda calma nuestro dolor (la muerte no vence). La tercera levanta nuestra esperanza a su altura (seremos semejantes a Cristo) — y ahí es donde el sermón debe culminar.

blocks.en: Before developing the peak point, let the first two questions be understood for what they are.
blocks.es_reference: Antes de desarrollar el punto culminante, entienda las dos primeras preguntas por lo que son.

blocks.en: 1. When will He come? — No one knows; be ready (Matthew 24:36, 44). “Of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but My Father only.” If the day was hidden even from the angels, the preacher who claims to have found it on a chart claims more than Scripture allows. History is full of the wreckage of those who tried: the Baptist lay-preacher William Miller worked the prophecies of Daniel and announced that Christ would return on October 22, 1844; tens of thousands believed him, some gave away all they had — and the day came and went, and it is remembered still as the Great Disappointment. The lesson is not that the promise failed but that the date-setters did. So Jesus draws the practical conclusion Himself: “Therefore you also be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.” The point of not knowing the day is not to make us calculate harder, but to make us live ready every day.
blocks.es_reference: 1. ¿Cuándo vendrá? — Nadie lo sabe; esté listo (Mateo 24:36, 44). “Pero del día y la hora nadie sabe, ni aun los ángeles de los cielos, sino solo mi Padre.” Si el día estuvo escondido aun de los ángeles, el predicador que dice haberlo hallado en una tabla reclama más de lo que la Escritura permite. La historia está llena de los restos de quienes lo intentaron: el predicador laico bautista William Miller trabajó las profecías de Daniel y anunció que Cristo volvería el 22 de octubre de 1844; decenas de miles le creyeron, algunos regalaron todo lo que tenían — y el día llegó y pasó, y se recuerda todavía como el Gran Chasco. La lección no es que la promesa fallara, sino que fallaron los que fijan fechas. Así que Jesús saca Él mismo la conclusión práctica: “Por tanto, también vosotros estad preparados; porque el Hijo del Hombre vendrá a la hora que no pensáis.” El punto de no saber el día no es hacernos calcular más, sino hacernos vivir listos cada día.

blocks.en: 2. What will happen when He comes? — The dead rise, we are gathered (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). “The Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a shout ... and the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them ... to meet the Lord in the air. And thus we shall always be with the Lord.” Here is the answer to the grave. Death does not get the last word over those who belong to Christ; it only holds them for a while, and at the shout it must give them back. Notice why Paul wrote it — not to feed speculation, but for comfort: “therefore comfort one another with these words.” This is the question to preach at the graveside, to the widow, to the parent who has buried a child: the One who is coming will raise our dead, and we shall all be together, and with Him, forever. And mark what rises: not a ghost, not a shadow, but the body itself, raised and made glorious — the same Christian hope that let the early church bury its dead facing the sunrise, in the sure expectation that the grave is a bed and not a grave at all. We do not merely survive death; we are raised out of it.
blocks.es_reference: 2. ¿Qué pasará cuando venga? — Los muertos resucitan, somos reunidos (1 Tesalonicenses 4:16–17). “El Señor mismo con voz de mando, con voz de arcángel, y con trompeta de Dios, descenderá del cielo; y los muertos en Cristo resucitarán primero. Luego nosotros los que vivimos, los que hayamos quedado, seremos arrebatados juntamente con ellos ... para recibir al Señor en el aire, y así estaremos siempre con el Señor.” He aquí la respuesta a la tumba. La muerte no tiene la última palabra sobre los que son de Cristo; solo los retiene por un tiempo, y a la voz de mando debe devolverlos. Note por qué lo escribió Pablo — no para alimentar la especulación, sino para consuelo: “por tanto, alentaos los unos a los otros con estas palabras.” Esta es la pregunta para predicar junto a la tumba, a la viuda, al padre que ha enterrado a un hijo: el que viene resucitará a nuestros muertos, y estaremos todos juntos, y con Él, para siempre. Y note qué resucita: no un fantasma, no una sombra, sino el cuerpo mismo, levantado y hecho glorioso — la misma esperanza cristiana que llevó a la iglesia primitiva a sepultar a sus muertos mirando hacia el amanecer, en la segura expectativa de que la tumba es un lecho y no una tumba en absoluto. No solo sobrevivimos a la muerte; somos levantados de ella.

blocks.en: 3. What will we become? — We shall be like Him (1 John 3:2). This is the height of the three, and we develop it in full below — the certainty that when we see Christ as He is, we shall at last be made like Him.
blocks.es_reference: 3. ¿Qué llegaremos a ser? — Seremos semejantes a Él (1 Juan 3:2). Esta es la altura de las tres, y la desarrollamos por completo abajo — la certeza de que cuando veamos a Cristo como Él es, seremos al fin hechos semejantes a Él.

blocks.en: Day 4 — Developing the Peak Point (E-A-I)
blocks.es_reference: Día 4 — Desarrollando el punto culminante (E-A-I)

blocks.en: Point 3, “What will we become?” (1 John 3:2), developed in full as the climax:
blocks.es_reference: El Punto 3, “¿Qué llegaremos a ser?” (1 Juan 3:2), desarrollado por completo como clímax:

blocks.en: Explanation of the text. “Beloved, now we are children of God; and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be, but we know that when He is revealed, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is.” John admits a mystery — we do not yet see the full picture — but he anchors one certainty: seeing Christ as He is, we shall be made like Him.
blocks.es_reference: Explicación del texto. “Amados, ahora somos hijos de Dios, y aún no se ha manifestado lo que hemos de ser; pero sabemos que cuando Él se manifieste, seremos semejantes a Él, porque le veremos como Él es.” Juan admite un misterio — aún no vemos el cuadro completo — pero ancla una certeza: al ver a Cristo como Él es, seremos hechos semejantes a Él.

blocks.en: Application of the text. So the Christian’s future is not vague survival but Christlikeness. This re-frames present struggle: every believer still fighting sin is on the way to a guaranteed likeness to Christ. The hope is not that we escape the world but that we are finally remade.
blocks.es_reference: Aplicación del texto. Así que el futuro del cristiano no es una vaga supervivencia sino la semejanza a Cristo. Esto re-enmarca la lucha presente: cada creyente que aún pelea contra el pecado va camino a una semejanza garantizada con Cristo. La esperanza no es que escapemos del mundo sino que al fin seamos rehechos.

blocks.en: Illustration. A photograph develops slowly; for a while the image is faint and unclear, but the picture was fixed the moment the shutter opened. We do not yet look like the final image, but in Christ it is already determined what we shall be. (Tell simply; do not overstate the science.)
blocks.es_reference: Ilustración. Una fotografía se revela despacio; por un tiempo la imagen es tenue y poco clara, pero el cuadro quedó fijado en el momento en que se abrió el obturador. Aún no nos parecemos a la imagen final, pero en Cristo ya está determinado lo que llegaremos a ser. (Cuéntelo con sencillez; no exagere la ciencia.)

blocks.en: 💡 The Last Trumpet: Paul says the trumpet will sound and the dead will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:52). A trumpet once called scattered people to gather; so the last trumpet gathers God’s scattered people, from every grave and every land, to their King.
blocks.es_reference: 💡 La Última Trompeta: Pablo dice que la trompeta sonará y los muertos resucitarán (1 Corintios 15:52). Una trompeta llamaba antes a la gente dispersa a reunirse; así la última trompeta reúne al pueblo disperso de Dios, de cada tumba y cada tierra, ante su Rey.

blocks.en: Day 5 — Craft Notes and the Close of the Course
blocks.es_reference: Día 5 — Notas de oficio y el cierre del curso

blocks.en: Three cautions, the first two especially for this doctrine. Do not preach a chart. Resist turning the sermon into date-setting or a survey of competing schemes; even where you hold a view, preach the certainties and hold the disputes humbly. (The Great Disappointment of 1844, told under Question 1, is the warning to cite.) Preach to both the grieving and the careless. The same return that comforts the mourner warns the complacent; reach both. Let the doctrine of hope arc to the invitation — because He is coming and we shall be like Him, the call is to be ready and to live now in the light of that day.
blocks.es_reference: Tres advertencias, las dos primeras especialmente para esta doctrina. No prediques un cuadro de fechas. Resiste convertir el sermón en fijar fechas o en un repaso de esquemas rivales; aun donde sostengas una postura, predica las certezas y sostén las disputas con humildad. (El Gran Chasco de 1844, contado en la Pregunta 1, es la advertencia que conviene citar.) Predica al que llora y al descuidado a la vez. El mismo regreso que consuela al doliente advierte al complaciente; alcanza a ambos. Deja que la doctrina de la esperanza se arquee hacia la invitación — porque Él viene y seremos semejantes a Él, el llamado es a estar listos y a vivir ahora a la luz de aquel día.

blocks.en: And so the course closes where preaching itself closes. You began in Unit 1 asking what doctrinal preaching is; you learned the method in Unit 2; and Units 3 through 10 ran that method across the whole body of Christian doctrine — each doctrine given a lean backbone, a subject and keyword, points anchored to texts, one point developed by Explanation, Application, and Illustration, and an arc toward response. The thesis held throughout: doctrinal preaching is topical and deductive, yet fully biblical, because every point rests on its own text. If you cannot find a text to preach the idea, it may be your idea and not the Lord’s. Go, and preach the whole counsel of God.
blocks.es_reference: Y así el curso cierra donde cierra la predicación misma. Comenzaste en la Unidad 1 preguntando qué es la predicación doctrinal; aprendiste el método en la Unidad 2; y las Unidades 3 a 10 corrieron ese método por todo el cuerpo de la doctrina cristiana — cada doctrina con un fundamento breve, un tema y una palabra clave, puntos anclados a textos, un punto desarrollado por Explicación, Aplicación e Ilustración, y un arco hacia la respuesta. La tesis se sostuvo en todo: la predicación doctrinal es tópica y deductiva, y a la vez plenamente bíblica, porque cada punto descansa en su propio texto. Si no puedes hallar un texto para predicar la idea, puede ser tu idea y no la del Señor. Ve, y predica todo el consejo de Dios.

blocks.en: "Even so, come, Lord Jesus!" — Revelation 22:20 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "¡Sí, ven, Señor Jesús!" — Apocalipsis 22:20 (RVG)

sa.prompt: Why is the doctrine of Last Things a fitting close to the course, and what is the pastoral aim of preaching it?
sa.model: Last Things is a fitting close because it is the doctrine of hope, the place where every faithful sermon finally points; the other doctrines unfold God’s work, and this one tells where it is all going, to the return of Christ and the world to come. The pastoral aim is the opposite of what the doctrine is often made into. Instead of a chart of dates or a contest of theories, the preacher aims to comfort the grieving with the certainty of resurrection, to sober the careless with the certainty of judgment, and above all to fix the hearer’s hope on Christ Himself rather than on a timeline.

sa.prompt: Summarize the doctrinal backbone of Last Things, distinguishing the certainties from the disputed details.
sa.model: The backbone holds several truths. Death is not the end but a doorway, so the believer who dies is absent from the body and present with the Lord. The return of Christ is personal, visible, and certain. The resurrection raises the body, so our hope is a redeemed and glorified body, not a disembodied soul. The judgment is real, for all will stand before God, and the final state is eternal, either the joy of God’s presence or the loss of it. The course distinguishes the certainties, that He will return, that the dead will rise, and that we shall be like Him, from the disputed details of timing and sequence, and it refuses to let those disputes crowd out the hope.

sa.prompt: Lay out the worked sermon: subject, keyword, and the three questions with their texts.
sa.model: The subject is the return of Christ, and the keyword is questions, since the doctrine answers the questions every honest heart asks, with three points each on its own text. The first question is when will He come, answered by Matthew 24:36 and 44: no one knows the day, so be ready. The second is what will happen when He comes, answered by 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17: the dead in Christ rise and we are gathered to Him. The third is what will we become, answered by 1 John 3:2: we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is. Three questions, three texts, one subject, arranged so the sermon rises to its peak at the third.

sa.prompt: Why does the deliberate order of the three questions matter? What does each one do for the hearer?
sa.model: The order matters because it shapes what the sermon does to the hearer. The first question, when will He come, humbles our curiosity, because we are deliberately not told the date and are simply commanded to be ready. The second question, what will happen, steadies our grief, because it shows that death does not win and the dead in Christ will rise. The third question, what will we become, lifts our hope to its height, because we shall be like Christ. Placing them in this order means the sermon does not end in mystery or in fear but peaks on the highest note, the hope of Christlikeness, which is exactly where a sermon on this doctrine should land.

sa.prompt: Develop “What will we become?” (1 John 3:2) using Explanation, Application, and Illustration.
sa.model: The Explanation is that John says now we are children of God and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be, but when Christ is revealed we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is; he admits a mystery, that we do not yet see the full picture, yet anchors one certainty, that seeing Christ we shall be made like Him. The Application is that the Christian’s future is not vague survival but Christlikeness, which re-frames present struggle, since every believer still fighting sin is on the way to a guaranteed likeness to Christ, and the hope is not escape from the world but being finally remade. The Illustration is a photograph that develops slowly, faint and unclear for a while, yet the image was fixed the moment the shutter opened, so in Christ it is already determined what we shall be even though we do not yet look like the final picture.

sa.prompt: How should the preacher handle the timing of Christ’s return, and why?
sa.model: The preacher should handle the timing with humility, because Scripture itself withholds the date. Matthew 24:36 says no one knows the day or the hour, and the command attached to that ignorance is simply to be ready. So the preacher must not turn the sermon into date-setting or a chart of competing schemes; even where he holds a particular view of sequence, he should preach the certainties and hold the disputed details humbly. History is full of failed date-setters, and if one is cited as a warning it should be verified and told briefly. The reason is pastoral and faithful at once: God gave us the certainty of the return precisely so that we would live ready, not so that we would calculate.

sa.prompt: Explain how a sermon on the return of Christ can address both the grieving and the careless.
sa.model: The same return of Christ speaks two ways at once, so one sermon can reach both kinds of hearer. To the grieving, the return is comfort: death does not win, the dead in Christ will rise, and those who mourn will see their believing loved ones again, so they do not grieve as those without hope. To the careless, the same return is a warning: He will come at an hour no one expects, and all will stand before God, so the complacent are roused to be ready. The preacher should hold both notes together rather than choosing one, letting the comfort steady the mourner and the warning awaken the complacent, because the one event genuinely carries both meanings.

sa.prompt: State the course’s central thesis about doctrinal preaching, as Unit 10 restates it.
sa.model: The thesis held across the whole course is that doctrinal preaching is topical and deductive, and yet fully biblical, because every point rests on its own text. The preacher gathers and arranges his points around a chosen subject, which makes the sermon topical, and he moves from the doctrine down to its parts, which makes it deductive; but it never floats free of Scripture, because each point is anchored to a passage. Unit 10 restates the test that guards this: if you cannot find a text to preach the idea, it may be your idea and not the Lord’s. That single sentence keeps doctrinal preaching honest, ensuring that what is preached as God’s truth actually comes from God’s Word.

sa.prompt: What is the photograph illustration, and what truth about the believer’s future does it carry?
sa.model: The photograph illustration is that a picture develops slowly, so that for a while the image is faint and unclear, yet the picture was actually fixed the moment the shutter opened. The truth it carries is that the believer’s future is already determined in Christ even though it is not yet fully seen. We do not yet look like the final image, and present struggle can make the outcome seem doubtful, but what we shall be was settled when we were joined to Christ, just as the photograph’s image was settled at the instant of exposure. So the believer can have confidence about a future that is certain though not yet visible, which is exactly the comfort 1 John 3:2 offers. Tell it simply, without overstating the science.

sa.prompt: Summarize how Units 3–10 ran a single method across the body of doctrine, and how Unit 10 closes the course.
sa.model: Units 3 through 10 ran one consistent method across the whole body of Christian doctrine. For each doctrine the unit gave a lean backbone drawn from systematic theology, then made the homiletical move with a subject, an interrogative, and a keyword, producing points each anchored to its own text, with one point developed by Explanation, Application, and Illustration, and the whole arced toward a response. The thesis held throughout: doctrinal preaching is topical and deductive yet fully biblical, because every point rests on a text. Unit 10 closes the course on the doctrine of hope, developing the worked outline first sketched in Unit 2 and peaking on the promise that we shall be like Christ, then sending the preacher out to preach the whole counsel of God by this method.
